name: PySceneDetect
purpose: Python library and CLI that detects shot boundaries in video using content, threshold, adaptive and histogram detectors, and can split video or export keyframes per scene.
journalism_use_case: First step in video verification: fragment an unknown clip into shots and pull one keyframe per shot so each frame can be reverse-image-searched, geolocated or compared against earlier uploads — the InVID/WeVerify keyframes workflow, runnable locally without uploading the video anywhere.
pros: Reproduces the single most useful verification workflow (keyframes for reverse search) entirely locally, which the InVID plugin cannot
Multiple detector algorithms with tunable thresholds, so you can handle both hard cuts and gradual transitions
Very actively maintained (v0.7.3, 2026-11-08; pushed 2026-11-17) with a large community (5,526 stars) and good documentation
BSD-3-Clause and scriptable, so it drops into a batch pipeline over an archive of collected video
cons: Detects cuts, not manipulation: it produces no authenticity judgement and no proof of anything — a point worth stating because shot-boundary anomalies get over-read
Content-based detection is threshold-sensitive and can over- or under-segment heavily compressed, low-light or shaky footage, which is most citizen video
Requires ffmpeg or mkvmerge for splitting, so deployment has an external dependency
61 open issues; tuning for a specific footage type takes experimentation
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,526 stars with 61 open issues, release v0.7.3 (2026-11-08), pushed 2026-11-17. The keyframe-per-shot workflow it enables is the documented basis of the InVID/WeVerify video-verification method.
assessment: Adopt — it is the local foundation of video verification and the reason you do not need to upload a sensitive clip to a third-party keyframe service. For your profile the workflow to standardise: yt-dlp to capture at full bitrate, MediaInfo to establish whether it is an original, PySceneDetect for keyframes, then local reverse-image comparison via your ImageHash/PDQ index before resorting to any external search engine.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.7.3 (2026-11-08), 5,526 stars, 61 open issues. Same-day commits and a recent release from a long-standing single maintainer with consistent cadence.
costs: No fee. CPU-bound; ffmpeg required for splitting. Negligible infrastructure.
privacy: Fully local — no network calls or API keys in the documented workflow, so the video never leaves your machine.
alternatives: Katna for keyframe selection optimised for visual quality — but note its stalled maintenance
ffmpeg scene-detection filters for a dependency-free approximation
InVID plugin for a one-click version that uploads the media
summary: Python library and CLI that detects shot boundaries in video using content, threshold, adaptive and histogram detectors…

name: Katna
purpose: Python library that selects representative keyframes from video by scoring frames for blur, brightness, contrast and visual diversity, and can also crop images intelligently.
journalism_use_case: Automatically pick the most informative, least blurry frames from shaky phone footage to use as geolocation and reverse-image-search candidates — the difference between reverse-searching a motion-blurred frame and a sharp one.
pros: Frame quality scoring (blur, brightness, contrast) is genuinely useful for geolocation work, where a sharp frame is worth ten blurry ones
Diversity-aware selection avoids returning ten near-identical frames from a static shot, which naive per-shot extraction does
MIT licensed with a small clean dependency set (OpenCV, FFmpeg) and no API keys
cons: Frame selection is optimised for visual appeal and diversity, not evidential completeness, so it can discard the one frame that matters — always verify against the full video, which is a real and easy-to-miss failure mode
Maintenance has stalled: last push 2024-08-06, no releases (tag v0.9.2), 401 stars — over two years quiet
Narrow scope: it chooses frames and does not detect shots, so it complements rather than replaces PySceneDetect
Small community means little guidance on parameter choice for investigative rather than thumbnail-generation use
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 401 stars with 10 open issues, no releases (tag v0.9.2), last push 2024-08-06, MIT licence. Its design intent (thumbnail and highlight selection) is documented by the project and explains the appeal-over-completeness bias.
assessment: Useful as a ranking aid on top of PySceneDetect's shot segmentation, not as a replacement for it — and never as a filter that decides which frames a human sees. For your profile the correct pattern is: PySceneDetect for all shot boundaries, Katna to rank frames within shots by quality, human review of the ranked list with the full video available. Given the dormancy I would not build anything load-bearing on it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-08-06, no releases, latest tag v0.9.2, 401 stars, 10 open issues. Over two years without activity; OpenCV-dependent code of this age will eventually break on new releases.
costs: No fee. CPU only; OpenCV and FFmpeg dependencies. Negligible.
alternatives: PySceneDetect for shot detection and keyframe export — maintained and the better foundation
A simple Laplacian-variance blur score written yourself, which is a few lines and removes the dependency
ffmpeg thumbnail filter for a crude equivalent
blockers: Dormant since 2024; frame selection optimises for appeal rather than completeness
summary: Python library that selects representative keyframes from video by scoring frames for blur, brightness…

name: Sherloq
purpose: Desktop GUI aggregating a wide set of image-forensics techniques — metadata inspection, error-level analysis, noise and JPEG-ghost maps, clone/copy-move detection, PCA and frequency analysis — in one local workbench.
journalism_use_case: A single local workbench to triage a suspicious photo: pull metadata, look for ELA, noise and JPEG-ghost anomalies, test for copy-move or splicing, and build a documented list of anomalies to take to further reporting — all without uploading the image anywhere.
pros: Breadth of techniques in one local GUI is the practical advantage: an analyst can run eight different tests in ten minutes rather than installing eight research repos
Fully local with no third-party service or API key documented, which matters enormously for unpublished or source-supplied imagery — the direct contrast with the InVID plugin's uploads
Largest community of any dedicated image-forensics GUI here (3,264 stars) with a modest backlog (25 open issues)
GPL-3.0 and inspectable, so the methods are auditable rather than black-box
cons: The author frames it as an educational and research toolkit rather than a definitive forgery detector — every panel output is a probabilistic signal requiring expert interpretation, NOT conclusive proof

ELA in particular is notoriously over-interpreted: it is the classic example of a forensic visualisation that looks compelling and proves little, and an analyst without training will produce false findings
Last push 2026-07-16 with no releases at all, so there is no version to pin and the project runs on a maintainer's spare attention
PySide2 and OpenCV dependencies of a certain vintage make installation fiddly on current systems
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,264 stars with 25 open issues, no releases, last push 2026-07-16; the author's own framing as an educational/research toolkit is stated in the repository. The over-interpretation risk of ELA is a well-established point in image-forensics literature, not a criticism specific to Sherloq.
assessment: Adopt it as the local alternative to uploading images to a forensics service, with a firm internal rule: outputs are leads for an analyst, never findings for a story, and no ELA image is ever published as evidence. For your profile its real value is privacy plus breadth — it lets you examine source-supplied imagery without disclosure. Pair with CAT-Net for a commercially usable model-based second opinion, and be realistic that interpreting these panels well requires training you may need to arrange.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-07-16, no releases or tags, 3,264 stars, 25 open issues. Four months since last push on a single-maintainer GUI; low backlog suggests attention, absence of releases suggests informal maintenance. Not declining, but the bus factor is one.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — classical signal-processing techniques, no trained models.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0; immaterial for desktop use by analysts.
costs: No fee. Runs on an analyst workstation; ExifTool binary and OpenCV required. Real cost is analyst training to interpret the outputs responsibly.
privacy: No third-party service or API key documented for the core tools; analysis runs locally, which is the decisive advantage for unpublished or source-sensitive imagery.
alternatives: PhotoHolmes for model-based localisation methods (with per-method licence caveats)
CAT-Net for a commercially usable splicing detector
InVID plugin for speed on already-public images, accepting the uploads
summary: Desktop GUI aggregating a wide set of image-forensics techniques — metadata inspection, error-level analysis…

name: c2pa-rs / c2patool
purpose: Rust implementation of the C2PA content-provenance specification, with a CLI (c2patool) for inspecting, validating and signing Content Credentials manifests embedded in media files.
journalism_use_case: Validate Content Credentials on images from C2PA-enabled cameras and tools to confirm a signed capture-and-edit chain, and sign the newsroom's own published assets so downstream users can verify they came from you unaltered — the only approach here that works by establishing provenance rather than guessing at manipulation.
pros: Provenance-based verification is structurally more reliable than detection: a valid signature chain is checkable evidence, whereas a detector score is a guess — and the detection field's in-the-wild failure rates make this the better bet
Signing your own published assets is a genuine newsroom capability: it lets partners and readers confirm an image came from you unmodified, which matters when your work is misappropriated
Very actively maintained (c2pa-c-ffi-v0.92.2 released 2026-11-16, pushed 2026-11-17) with dual Apache-2.0 OR MIT licensing
Industry-backed specification with camera and tool vendors implementing it, so coverage will grow rather than shrink
cons: Only informative for files that carry credentials, and absence of a manifest is extremely common and means nothing — most media you encounter will have no credentials at all, which limits present-day utility
A valid signature proves who signed and the declared edit history, not that the depicted events occurred — a distinction that will be misunderstood as C2PA becomes more visible
Signing requires certificates and a trust list, so there is real PKI work and key management before you can sign your own assets
310 open issues against 449 stars and a confusing release scheme (per-crate tags), so integration takes orientation; GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION for the dual licence
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 449 stars with 310 open issues, release c2pa-c-ffi-v0.92.2 (2026-11-16), pushed 2026-11-17, dual Apache-2.0 OR MIT with SPDX NOASSERTION. The specification's industry backing is evidenced by the Content Authenticity Initiative's membership, though actual camera-side coverage in the wild was not measured in this survey.
assessment: Worth integrating now on the signing side and monitoring on the validation side. Concretely for your profile: start signing published images, because that capability compounds in value and costs only PKI setup; treat validation as a bonus that occasionally helps rather than a workflow you can rely on, since most material carries no manifest. The strategic point is that provenance is the only verification approach whose reliability improves over time, while detection's degrades as generators improve.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release c2pa-c-ffi-v0.92.2 (2026-11-16), 449 stars, 310 open issues. Same-day commits and near-daily releases across crates; industry-funded maintenance. The large backlog reflects an evolving specification rather than neglect.
licence: Apache-2.0 OR MIT (dual; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Trust lists and certificates are governed by the issuing authorities' terms.
licence_restrictions: Dual permissive licensing — choose either and record the choice. The practical constraints are PKI-related: obtaining a certificate recognised by the relevant trust list is a governance question, not a licence one.
costs: No software fee. Signing requires a certificate: costs depend on the issuing authority and were NOT verified in this survey. Rust toolchain for building; negligible runtime cost. No GPU.
privacy: Local validation of embedded manifests, with an optional network fetch for trust-list checks — so validation can be done offline if you pre-stage the trust list. Note that signing embeds assertions about your newsroom's tools and workflow into published files, so review what the manifest discloses before signing.
alternatives: Signing with standard detached signatures plus published hashes, if C2PA's complexity is unjustified
Community Forensics or CAT-Net for detection-based approaches, with their much weaker reliability
ExifTool plus MediaInfo for the pre-C2PA provenance signals that remain useful
summary: Rust implementation of the C2PA content-provenance specification, with a CLI (c2patool) for inspecting…

name: VFRAME
purpose: Computer-vision toolkit for human-rights investigation, providing object-detection pipelines over large video archives with custom models trained for specific munitions and objects.
journalism_use_case: Triage very large conflict-footage archives by flagging frames likely to contain a specific object, such as a cluster-munition remnant, so investigators review a shortlist instead of thousands of hours of video — work that is otherwise simply not done because nobody can watch it all.
pros: Purpose-built for human-rights investigation rather than adapted from generic CV, with custom models for munitions identification — a genuinely unusual and valuable specialisation
Addresses an intractable problem: conflict-footage archives are too large to review manually, so a shortlist is the difference between evidence found and evidence lost
MIT licensed with local processing of local archives, appropriate for sensitive material
The methodology (train a detector for a specific object class relevant to one investigation) is reusable even if the code is not
cons: Long dormancy: last push 2023-05-28, no releases, 76 stars — three and a half years quiet, and dependency rot in a deep-learning project of that age is near-certain
Detector outputs are probabilistic signals requiring human confirmation of every hit, never conclusive identification — and misidentifying a munition type in print would be a serious error
Custom models are domain-specific and may not be distributed with the repository, so the capability depends on model availability not just code
NVIDIA GPU strongly recommended, and the deep-learning runtime of that era will need pinning or rebuilding
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 76 stars with 0 open issues, no releases, last push 2023-05-28, MIT licence. The project's human-rights-investigation orientation is documented on vframe.io; VFRAME's munitions-detection work is known in the open-source-investigation community, though I verified no specific deployment.
assessment: Reference only as software, but important as a methodology for your work. The idea — train a narrow detector for the specific object an investigation turns on, and use it to produce a review shortlist — is sound and reproducible today with maintained tooling (YOLO-family models, or a fine-tuned vision model) in far less time than reviving a 2023 pipeline. If you have a conflict-footage archive problem, I would rebuild the approach rather than the code, and keep human confirmation of every hit as an absolute rule.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2023-05-28, no releases or tags, 76 stars, 0 open issues. Three and a half years without activity on a deep-learning project; the dependency stack of that period (CUDA, framework versions) makes reuse a porting exercise.
model_or_data_licence: Custom detection models are domain-specific and may be distributed separately; their terms were not verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Model availability and terms are the open question.
costs: No fee. NVIDIA GPU strongly recommended; no paid API. The real cost would be training a detector for your object class — annotation labour plus GPU time. Estimate.
privacy: Local processing of local archives, which is essential for conflict footage that may identify victims or witnesses.
alternatives: A fine-tuned modern object detector (YOLO-family) built with maintained tooling for the same purpose
Bellingcat smart-image-sorter for zero-shot triage without training
Atlos for the collaborative verification workflow around such archives
blockers: Dormant since 2023; deep-learning dependency stack requires porting
summary: Computer-vision toolkit for human-rights investigation, providing object-detection pipelines over large video archives with…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure; staff effort

name: Bellingcat smart-image-sorter
purpose: CLI that classifies images into user-defined categories using zero-shot vision-language models, sorting a directory of images into labelled folders.
journalism_use_case: Triage a large unsorted image dump by describing the categories you care about in plain words — 'military vehicle', 'street protest', 'document scan' — and letting the model bucket images for review, turning an unreviewable folder into a prioritised queue.
pros: Zero-shot labels mean no training data and no annotation, so an analyst can define investigation-specific categories in minutes
Runs locally after weight download with no paid API, so a sensitive image dump is not uploaded anywhere
Apache-2.0 and simple enough to adapt; built by Bellingcat for practising investigators
GPU helpful but not required, so it works on an analyst workstation
cons: Zero-shot classification is an unreliable triage aid, not a labelling authority: accuracy varies sharply with label wording and it fails on fine-grained military or technical distinctions — exactly the distinctions investigations often need
Every bucket needs human review, so it reorders work rather than reducing it — valuable, but not the labour saving people expect
Dormant: last push 2024-08-14, no releases, 68 stars — over two years quiet, and the underlying model landscape has moved considerably since
Model weights are GB-scale downloads, which is a practical constraint on a field machine
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 68 stars means minimal community signal. Documented: no releases, last push 2024-08-14, Apache-2.0. The accuracy limitations of zero-shot classification on fine-grained categories are a documented property of the method rather than a defect of this implementation.
assessment: The idea is right and the implementation is stale. For your profile I would reimplement the same pattern against a current vision-language model — it is a short script — and gain substantially better accuracy, since zero-shot classification has improved markedly since 2024. Keep the core discipline either way: the model produces a review order, never a label you act on, and fine-grained technical identification (which munition, which uniform) must be done by a human expert.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-08-14, no releases or tags, 68 stars, 0 open issues. Over two years without activity; because the value depends on the underlying model, staleness here means using a model generation behind what is available.
model_or_data_licence: Depends on the vision-language model selected; weights fetched from third-party hubs and not individually verified in this survey.

costs: No fee and no paid API. GB-scale model weight download; GPU helpful but not required. Estimate.
privacy: Local inference after weights download; images are not uploaded if run locally, which is the property that makes it usable on a sensitive dump.
alternatives: Reimplementing the pattern with a current vision-language model — recommended
imagededup first, to collapse duplicates before classification
VFRAME's approach (a trained narrow detector) where a specific object class matters and accuracy is critical

additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: GeoCLIP
purpose: CLIP-based model that predicts GPS coordinates for an image by aligning image embeddings with a learned location embedding space, returning ranked candidate locations.
journalism_use_case: Narrowing the search space when geolocating a photo with no metadata: GeoCLIP proposes candidate regions, which an investigator then confirms or rejects by matching buildings, signage, vegetation and terrain against satellite and street-level imagery. It replaces 'somewhere in the world' with 'check these three regions first'.
pros: Dramatically narrows the search space, which is the real bottleneck in manual geolocation — an investigator with three candidate regions can work; one with none cannot
MIT licensed with pretrained weights distributed in the package, so there is no separate weights-licence trap
Inference is local once installed, so case images need not be sent to a geolocation API — a significant privacy advantage over hosted services
Actively maintained (v1.3.0 released 2026-10-25, same-day push)
cons: Produces a probabilistic guess over coordinates, NEVER a location fact or proof — and the README states no per-image accuracy figures, so you cannot quantify confidence for a specific photo

Biased toward locations well represented in training data, which means tourist and urban scenes work far better than rural areas in under-photographed countries — precisely where much conflict reporting happens
Benchmark accuracy says nothing about any individual image, and a confident-looking top candidate can be entirely wrong
Narrow function: it proposes, it does not verify, so the labour-intensive confirmation step remains entirely manual
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 420 stars with 9 open issues, release v1.3.0 on 2026-10-25 with same-day push, MIT licence with weights distributed in the package; the README's absence of per-image accuracy figures is itself the relevant disclosure.
assessment: Adopt as a search-space-narrowing aid with a hard rule that its output never appears in a story as a location claim. For your profile the honest framing for reporters is: GeoCLIP tells you where to look, satellite and street-level imagery tell you where it is. Be especially sceptical of its output for rural locations in under-represented regions, which is where the training bias bites and where its confidence is least warranted.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-25, latest release v1.3.0 published the same day, 420 stars, 9 open issues. Recent release with a clean tracker; research-origin project sustaining a release cadence.

licence_restrictions: None identified. Note the model derives from CLIP, whose own terms flow through in principle — worth checking if you redistribute weights.
costs: No fee. PyTorch plus CLIP backbone; GPU helpful. Weights download on first use. Estimate.
privacy: Inference is local once installed, so case images need not be sent to a geolocation API — the decisive advantage over hosted image-geolocation services, which would receive your unpublished imagery.
alternatives: ShadowFinder for shadow-based chronolocation when a shadow and timestamp are visible
Manual geolocation against satellite imagery and Mapillary/street-level panoramas
LoFTR or hloc for feature-matching a candidate location against reference imagery
summary: CLIP-based model that predicts GPS coordinates for an image by aligning image embeddings with a learned location embedding space…

name: ShadowFinder
purpose: Tool that computes the set of possible locations consistent with an observed shadow length and a known timestamp, or the set of possible times consistent with a shadow at a known location, producing a map of candidate bands.
journalism_use_case: Classic chronolocation and geolocation: given a photo with a visible shadow and a claimed timestamp, narrow the possible latitudes and longitudes — or run it in reverse to test whether a claimed location and time are physically consistent with the shadow in the image. The reverse test is the stronger journalistic move, because it can falsify a claim outright.
pros: Grounded in astronomy rather than machine learning, so the result is a deterministic physical constraint rather than a probabilistic guess — qualitatively stronger evidence than any model output here
The reverse mode (test a claimed location and time for consistency) can falsify a claim, which is rarer and more valuable than narrowing a search
MIT licensed, actively released (0.7.1 on 2026-09-03, same-day push), built by Bellingcat for practising investigators
The Python/CLI route runs entirely locally and takes measurements as input, not the image itself — so nothing sensitive leaves the machine
cons: Output is a probabilistic band of candidate locations, not a point and not proof, and is only as good as its inputs: object height and shadow length must be estimated from the image, and that estimation is usually the dominant error source
Requires a visible, measurable shadow with a known or estimable object height — a minority of photographs qualify

The recommended Google Colab route executes in Google's cloud, which means the measurements (and potentially the image, if uploaded there) leave your control — use the local CLI instead for sensitive cases
Narrow applicability and 13 open issues on a small project (628 stars)
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 628 stars with 13 open issues, release 0.7.1 on 2026-09-03 with same-day push, MIT licence; the Colab-based workflow is documented by the project. Shadow-based chronolocation is an established technique in open-source investigation practice.
assessment: Adopt, and prefer the local CLI over the documented Colab route — that is the single most important operational point, because Colab puts your measurements and possibly the image into Google's infrastructure. For your profile the highest-value use is falsification: when a government or a propaganda account claims a video was shot at a given place and time, shadow geometry can show it was not, and that is a publishable finding grounded in physics rather than in a model's opinion. Document your height and length estimates, since they carry the error.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-03, latest release 0.7.1 published the same day, 628 stars, 13 open issues. Recent release from an institutional maintainer (Bellingcat) with a clean tracker.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — astronomical computation, no trained model. Depends on suncalc and timezone grid data.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute; runs on a laptop. The Colab route is free within Google's limits but is the option to avoid for sensitive work.
privacy: The Python/CLI route runs entirely locally and takes measurements rather than the image itself — an excellent privacy position. The recommended Colab route executes in Google's cloud and should be avoided for unpublished material.
alternatives: SunCalc or Skyfield for the underlying solar-position computation if you build your own tooling
GeoCLIP to narrow the region before applying shadow constraints
Stellarium for verifying night-sky rather than solar geometry
summary: Tool that computes the set of possible locations consistent with an observed shadow length and a known timestamp…

name: SunCalc
purpose: Tiny JavaScript library computing sun and moon position, sunrise/sunset and twilight phases, and lunar illumination for a given date and location.
journalism_use_case: The primitive behind shadow and lighting verification: given a claimed location and timestamp, compute where the sun should have been and check whether shadow direction, length and light quality in the photo agree — a cheap, strong consistency test that can contradict a claimed time or place.
pros: Deterministic astronomical computation, so the result is a physical fact rather than an estimate — the strongest epistemic footing available in image verification
Extremely small and dependency-free, trivially embeddable in a newsroom verification tool or a browser-side check
BSD-2-Clause, actively released (v2.1.4 on 2026-11-10, same-day push) with a large user base (3,514 stars) and a tiny backlog (10 open issues)
Pure computation with no network calls, so it is safe to run client-side on sensitive cases
cons: It computes astronomy, not verification: it cannot tell you anything about the image, and all the interpretive work remains yours

A 'mismatch' is a probabilistic indication that may reflect a wrong coordinate, a wrong timezone assumption, terrain shadowing or an obstruction rather than a false claim — timezone errors in particular are the classic self-inflicted wound
JavaScript-first, so a Python pipeline needs suncalc-py or an equivalent port
Does not handle atmospheric refraction edge cases or complex terrain, so near-horizon calculations need care
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 3,514 stars with 10 open issues, release v2.1.4 on 2026-11-10 with same-day push, BSD-2-Clause. Widely used as the computation layer in geolocation tooling, including ShadowFinder's dependency on suncalc.
assessment: Integrate it as the computational core of any lighting or shadow verification you build — and the reason to use it rather than reimplementing is simply that solar-position maths is easy to get subtly wrong. For your profile the practical warning is timezone handling: most false 'inconsistencies' in shadow analysis come from a wrong UTC offset or an unaccounted daylight-saving change, so make the timezone explicit and record it in the methodology note.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-10, latest release v2.1.4 published the same day, 3,514 stars, 10 open issues. Recent release on a long-stable library from a well-known maintainer; minimal backlog.
costs: No fee, no dependencies, no infrastructure.
privacy: Pure computation with no network calls; safe to run client-side on sensitive cases.
alternatives: suncalc-py for a Python port of the same calculations
Skyfield for higher-precision astronomy including star and planet positions
ShadowFinder, which wraps this computation into an investigative workflow
summary: Tiny JavaScript library computing sun and moon position, sunrise/sunset and twilight phases…
